overview: This section covers the four Elastic Load Balancing types: Classic Load Balancer (v1), Application Load Balancer (v2, Layer 7), Network Load Balancer (v2, Layer 4) and Gateway Load Balancer (Layer 3). The exam repeatedly asks you to pick the right type from scenario clues such as protocol (HTTP/HTTPS vs TCP/UDP vs IP packets), need for advanced routing, need for static IPs, extreme performance, or third-party appliance inspection — so learn each type's layer, features and limits as a decision matrix, not a list.

coreConcepts.definition: Legacy load balancer that supports TCP (Layer 4) and HTTP/HTTPS (Layer 7) with TCP- or HTTP-based health checks and a fixed hostname XXX.region.elb.amazonaws.com.
Layer 7 (HTTP) load balancer for routing HTTP/HTTPS traffic to multiple applications and target groups, with support for HTTP/2, WebSocket and redirects such as HTTP to HTTPS.
ALB routes requests to different target groups based on path in the URL, hostname in the URL, query string parameters, or headers.
Routing on the URL path, e.g. example.com/users to one target group and example.com/posts to another.
Routing on the hostname in the URL, e.g. one.example.com vs other.example.com to different target groups.
Routing on query string parameters (e.g. example.com/users?id=123&order=false) or HTTP headers, e.g. ?Platform=Mobile vs ?Platform=Desktop to different target groups.
EC2 instances (optionally in an Auto Scaling Group), ECS tasks, Lambda functions (HTTP request translated into a JSON event) and IP addresses (must be private IPs).
For an ALB, health checks are configured at the target group level, not per load balancer.
ALB feature that redirects to a dynamic port in ECS, enabling load balancing to multiple applications/containers on the same machine.

Header inserted by the ALB carrying the true client IP, because application servers only see the load balancer's private IP (connection termination). X-Forwarded-Port and X-Forwarded-Proto give port and protocol.
Layer 4 load balancer that forwards TCP and UDP traffic, handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency, and has one static IP per AZ with support for Elastic IPs.
EC2 instances, IP addresses (must be private IPs) and an Application Load Balancer; NLB health checks support TCP, HTTP and HTTPS.
Layer 3 (IP packet) load balancer that deploys, scales and manages fleets of third-party network virtual appliances such as firewalls, IDS/IPS and deep packet inspection systems.
Combines a transparent network gateway (a single entry/exit point for all traffic, used with route tables) with a load balancer that distributes traffic to the virtual appliances.
The encapsulation protocol used by Gateway Load Balancer on port 6081 to send traffic to the appliances.
EC2 instances and IP addresses (must be private IPs).
Both CLB and ALB expose a fixed DNS name of the form XXX.region.elb.amazonaws.com.
The load balancer terminates the client connection, so backend EC2 instances do not see the client IP directly.

mustRemember: CLB is the only type described as supporting both TCP (Layer 4) and HTTP/HTTPS (Layer 7); ALB is Layer 7 only; NLB is Layer 4 (TCP and UDP); GWLB is Layer 3 (IP packets).
NLB provides one static IP per AZ and supports assigning Elastic IPs — the choice when a customer must whitelist specific IPs.
NLB handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency — the choice for extreme performance and TCP/UDP.
ALB routing can be based on path, hostname, query string and headers — CLB cannot do this; you would need multiple CLBs per application.
ALB target groups can be EC2 instances, ECS tasks, Lambda functions, or IP addresses; IP addresses in ALB, NLB and GWLB target groups must be private IPs.
For Lambda targets, the ALB translates the HTTP request into a JSON event.
Application servers behind an ALB see the load balancer's private IP, not the client IP; the true client IP is in the X-Forwarded-For header (plus X-Forwarded-Port and X-Forwarded-Proto).
ALB health checks are at the target group level; NLB health checks support TCP, HTTP and HTTPS.
GWLB uses the GENEVE protocol on port 6081 and acts as a transparent network gateway (single entry/exit) combined with a load balancer for third-party virtual appliances.
GWLB appliances are examples like firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention systems, and deep packet inspection / payload manipulation systems.
CLB health checks are TCP or HTTP based; CLB and ALB both have a fixed hostname XXX.region.elb.amazonaws.com.
NLB can have an ALB as a target group — a common pattern for static IP/private connectivity in front of Layer 7 routing.

keyComparisons.difference: ALB is Layer 7 with content-based routing and HTTP/2/WebSocket; NLB is Layer 4 for TCP/UDP at extreme performance with static IPs per AZ.
CLB is the legacy v1 with one application per load balancer and fixed hostname, whereas ALB gives path/hostname/query string/header routing to multiple target groups.
ALB distributes HTTP requests to application targets; GWLB sends IP packets (Layer 3) through third-party security appliances using GENEVE on port 6081.
Both are non-HTTP, but NLB (Layer 4, TCP/UDP) balances traffic to your applications while GWLB (Layer 3) inserts virtual appliances transparently into the traffic path via route tables.
ALB supports EC2, ECS tasks, Lambda and private IPs; NLB supports EC2, private IPs and an ALB; GWLB supports EC2 and private IPs.

keyComparisons.items: ALB vs CLB client IP visibility
keyComparisons.difference: Both terminate connections so backends see the load balancer IP, but only the ALB/documented header approach (X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Port, X-Forwarded-Proto) is called out in this section for recovering client IP, port and protocol.

keyComparisons.items: ALB vs NLB for IP whitelisting
keyComparisons.difference: NLB offers one static IP per AZ and Elastic IP assignment for whitelisting; ALB exposes only a fixed DNS hostname whose IPs are not static.

commonMisunderstandings: NLB is not HTTP-aware for routing: it forwards TCP and UDP traffic, so path- or hostname-based routing belongs to ALB.
ALB does not let backend servers see the client IP directly; the client IP must be read from the X-Forwarded-For header.
Target group IP addresses must be private IPs — you cannot register public IPs as ALB, NLB or GWLB targets.
Yes, an NLB can target an ALB — NLB target groups are not limited to EC2 and IP addresses.
Lambda cannot be a target of an NLB or GWLB in this section; Lambda target groups are an ALB feature.
GWLB is not a Layer 4 TCP/UDP balancer for your app tier — it operates at Layer 3 on IP packets to insert appliances.
ALB health checks are defined at the target group level, so different target groups can be checked independently.
mentalModels: Think of CLB as the old single-lane highway, ALB as a traffic officer reading the URL sign, NLB as a high-speed rail for raw packets, and GWLB as a security checkpoint every packet must pass through.
ALB = look inside the request (path, host, query, header); NLB = look only at the packet (TCP/UDP); GWLB = look at the IP packet and detour it to appliances.
X-Forwarded-For is the envelope the ALB sticks on the request so the backend can see who really sent it.
NLB static IP per AZ = one doorman per building entrance, ideal when partners must whitelist your address.
edgeCases: ALB port mapping redirects to a dynamic port in ECS, which is what lets one ALB serve many container tasks instead of needing one CLB per application.
ALB supports redirects (for example HTTP to HTTPS), HTTP/2 and WebSocket.
NLB health checks may be TCP, HTTP or HTTPS even though traffic forwarding is TCP/UDP.
GWLB combines two roles: transparent network gateway (single entry/exit) plus load balancer to the appliance fleet; route tables direct traffic to it.
ALB query string routing can select targets on application-level values such as ?Platform=Mobile vs ?Platform=Desktop, even routing to on-premises private IPs.

whenToUse.situation: Legacy application needing simple TCP or HTTP/HTTPS balancing with a fixed hostname
Microservices or container apps needing routing by path, hostname, query string or header
Need to route to Lambda, or to a mix of EC2, ECS tasks and private IPs
Requirements for millions of requests per second, ultra-low latency, TCP or UDP
Partners must whitelist specific IPs; need one static IP per AZ / Elastic IP
Need third-party firewalls, IDS/IPS or deep packet inspection in the traffic path
Need a static IP entry point in front of Layer 7 routing
whenToUse.use: NLB with an ALB as its target group

patternsToRecognize.signal: The backend must know the client's IP address
Route example.com/users to one service and example.com/posts to another
Whitelist specific IPs or static IP per AZ
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Network Load Balancer with Elastic IPs

patternsToRecognize.signal: Millions of requests per second, ultra-low latency, UDP
Deploy firewalls / IDS / IPS virtual appliances, GENEVE port 6081
One load balancer serving multiple Docker containers with dynamic ports on ECS
HTTP request turned into a JSON event
Multiple applications per Classic Load Balancer
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Wrong — a CLB per application; use ALB instead

examTraps.trap: Using a CLB for path-based routing to microservices
examTraps.correction: Only the ALB supports path/hostname/query string/header routing; a CLB would need one load balancer per application.

examTraps.trap: Choosing NLB because it 'supports HTTP routing'
examTraps.correction: NLB is Layer 4 TCP/UDP; content-based HTTP routing is ALB. NLB may sit in front of an ALB for static IPs.

examTraps.trap: Registering a public IP as an ALB/NLB target IP
examTraps.correction: Target group IP addresses must be private IPs.

examTraps.trap: Reading the client IP directly from the packet at the application server behind an ALB
examTraps.correction: Connection termination means the server sees the load balancer IP; use X-Forwarded-For (plus X-Forwarded-Port/Proto).

examTraps.trap: Picking GWLB for ordinary TCP/UDP application balancing
examTraps.correction: GWLB is Layer 3 for inserting third-party virtual appliances; use NLB for TCP/UDP application traffic.

examTraps.trap: Confusing health-check protocols: assuming NLB only does TCP checks
examTraps.correction: NLB health checks support TCP, HTTP and HTTPS.

examTraps.trap: Assuming ALB health checks are per load balancer
examTraps.correction: ALB health checks are configured at the target group level.

examTraps.trap: Expecting X-Forwarded-For from a Gateway Load Balancer appliance flow
examTraps.correction: X-Forwarded-For is an ALB (HTTP) feature; GWLB works on Layer 3 IP packets via GENEVE on port 6081.

beyondSource: SAA-C03 exam guide (Domain 3, Task 3.4, and Domain 4, Task 4.2) explicitly frames load balancing as 'selecting the appropriate load balancing strategy', and contrasts ALB (Layer 7) vs NLB (Layer 4) vs Gateway Load Balancer — matching the four-type decision focus of this section.
